uncited: It is distinguished from sibling methods like [Load-Balanced Cell Assignment](4194-load-balanced-cell-assignment.md) by operating on the image plane rather than the volume data space, and from [Farm on Demand (FD)](7455-farm-on-demand-fd.md) by its static, cyclic assignment rather than dynamic task queuing.
- Image dimensions: width $W$, height $H$ (number of scanlines).
- Assignment map: For each pixel $(x, y)$, the ID of the processor responsible for merging its ray segments.
Assign all pixels $(x, y)$ for $0 \le x < W$ to the calculated `processor_id`.
- When using a large number of processors ($P$ is large relative to $H$), scanline interleaving may fail to distribute high-density regions effectively.
- The method assumes that the vertical distribution of depth complexity is relatively uniform.
A finer-grained variant where individual pixels (or small blocks) are assigned in round-robin order rather than entire scanlines.
It is chosen when the number of processors is large relative to the image height, or when depth complexity is highly localized.
It offers better load balancing at the cost of increased communication overhead for small pixel blocks.
See [Scanline Interleaving](#scanline-interleaving) for the base method.
- **Time Complexity**: $O(W \times H)$ for the assignment phase, where $W$ and $H$ are image dimensions.
The merging phase is proportional to the number of ray segments per pixel, which is balanced across processors by the partitioning.
It does not account for horizontal variations in depth complexity.
- **When to Use**: When $H \gg P$ and depth complexity is relatively uniform across horizontal bands.
- **When Not to Use**: When $P$ is large relative to $H$, or when depth complexity is clustered in specific horizontal regions.
Use Pixel Interleaving or [Hybrid Image Partitioning](7675-hybrid-image-partending.md) instead.
